Gauge-calibrated proportion mediated: the residual W

Source: vignettes/gauge-residual.qmd

The problem with a single proportion-mediated number

The interventional proportion mediated P_med = IIE / OE summarizes mediation in one number. That summary is only trustworthy when the overall effect decomposes additively into a direct and an indirect part. With a treatment-by-mediator interaction (or intermediate confounding) the additive split fails: there is a leftover

R=OE−IDE−IIE, R = \mathrm{OE} - \mathrm{IDE} - \mathrm{IIE},

the non-decomposability remainder. When RR is nonzero, IIE / OE is reporting a fraction of a quantity that was never the sum of its parts.

ward_residual() estimates P_med and the gauge residual

W=R/OE, W = R / \mathrm{OE},

a scale-free flag for that failure. W≈0W \approx 0 certifies the additive split; a WW significantly away from 0 says “interpret P_med with care.”

library(probmed)

A clean (additive) example

With no interaction term, RR — and hence WW — should sit at zero, and the gauge P_med agrees with the usual story.

n <- 1500
C <- rnorm(n)
A <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.2 + 0.8 * C))
M <- 0.6 * A + 0.4 * C + rnorm(n)
Y <- 0.5 * A + 0.7 * M + 0.3 * C + rnorm(n)        # no A*M term
ward_residual(data.frame(A, M, Y, C))
#> Gauge-calibrated proportion mediated (onestep-crossfit, n=1500)
#>   P_med = 0.446  Wald [0.355, 0.538]
#>     Fieller 95% CI [0.357, 0.542]
#>   W=R/OE = 0.059  Wald [-0.031, 0.150]  (p=0.199)
#>   OE=0.971  IDE=0.480  IIE=0.433  R=0.058

The W confidence interval covers 0: the single-number P_med is safe here.

An interaction breaks the split

Add an A * M term and the gauge lights up — W is now significantly positive and the printout warns that the additive split is unreliable.

Yi <- 0.5 * A + 0.7 * M + 0.8 * A * M + 0.3 * C + rnorm(n)
ward_residual(data.frame(A, M, Y = Yi, C))
#> Gauge-calibrated proportion mediated (onestep-crossfit, n=1500)
#>   P_med = 0.322  Wald [0.264, 0.380]
#>     Fieller 95% CI [0.264, 0.381]
#>   W=R/OE = 0.444  Wald [0.337, 0.550]  (p=3.41e-16)
#>   OE=1.423  IDE=0.333  IIE=0.459  R=0.632
#>   ! |W| large: additive split unreliable; interpret P_med with care.

Non-binary-coded exposures: a0 / a1

The treatment need not be coded 0/1. Any two-level coding works — a factor, {1, 2}, {-1, 1} — by naming the reference a0 and comparison a1. A is recoded internally to the indicator (A == a1).

dat <- data.frame(A = factor(ifelse(A == 1, "drug", "placebo")),
                  M = M, Y = Yi, C = C)
ward_residual(dat, a0 = "placebo", a1 = "drug")
#> Gauge-calibrated proportion mediated (onestep-crossfit, n=1500)
#>   P_med = 0.322  Wald [0.264, 0.380]
#>     Fieller 95% CI [0.264, 0.381]
#>   W=R/OE = 0.444  Wald [0.337, 0.550]  (p=3.41e-16)
#>   OE=1.423  IDE=0.333  IIE=0.459  R=0.632
#>   ! |W| large: additive split unreliable; interpret P_med with care.

W = R / OE is anti-symmetric in the contrast direction: swapping a0 and a1 flips the sign of W (the remainder R is invariant, OE changes sign) while leaving its magnitude — the thing you interpret — unchanged.

A treatment with more than two levels is rejected rather than silently subsetted: restricting the data to two of several levels would change the population the corner means are averaged over, estimating a different (sub-population) gauge. Filter to the two levels you intend to contrast first.

multi <- data.frame(A = sample(0:2, n, replace = TRUE), M = M, Y = Yi, C = C)
ward_residual(multi, a0 = 0, a1 = 1)
#> Error:
#> ! A has more than two levels (extra: {2}). ward_residual contrasts exactly two levels; subsetting a multi-valued A would change the estimand. Pre-filter to the two levels you intend, or see the manuscript for the multi-valued generalization (not yet implemented).

Inference: what the two arms actually do

W and P_med are ratios. The default se_method = "analytic" reports the influence-function standard error of the cross-fit one-step estimator and a symmetric Wald interval. Measured against exact truth (inst/sim/se_shipped_check.R, 250 datasets per cell, n = 800) it covers 0.936 for a continuous outcome and 0.972 for a binary one under strong identification, 0.912 when the total effect is moderate, and its dispersion from dataset to dataset matches that of an oracle that knows the nuisance functions. reps > 1 averages the influence matrix over several independent partitions; it removes the fold-split component of the variance, which with correct weights is small (empSD 0.063 at reps = 1 vs 0.061 at reps = 10, oracle 0.056):

ward_residual(data.frame(A, M, Y = Yi, C), reps = 10)
#> Gauge-calibrated proportion mediated (onestep-crossfit, n=1500)
#>   P_med = 0.327  Wald [0.269, 0.384]
#>     Fieller 95% CI [0.269, 0.385]
#>   W=R/OE = 0.437  Wald [0.332, 0.543]  (p=5.12e-16)
#>   OE=1.410  IDE=0.332  IIE=0.461  R=0.617
#>   ! |W| large: additive split unreliable; interpret P_med with care.

A note on history, because the earlier documentation said the opposite: before 2026-08-22 the corner influence function used one inverse-probability weight per fold — ifelse() on a scalar test silently returned the first fold row’s propensity for every row — and every coverage figure the package reported (Wald ~0.85–0.90, percentile ~1.00, the gate-validation grid, the variance decomposition in docs/specs/FINDINGS-2026-08-22-phi-decomposition.md) was produced with that bug. Those numbers are superseded; the bootstrap arm and the two gates were re-measured the same day (docs/specs/FINDINGS-2026-08-22-postfix-bootstrap-gates.md).

Setting se_method = "bootstrap" switches the W and P_med intervals to percentile intervals of a nonparametric bootstrap that resamples rows and refits the whole cross-fit, with a fresh partition each resample. With correct weights it buys nothing: percentile coverage 0.905–0.930 in the regular cells at the same width as the Wald interval, and a bootstrap standard error that is unstable for binary outcomes. It remains available for users who want a refit bootstrap. The weak_id flag it enables — percentile interval at least 3× wider than Wald — is a symptom of bootstrap instability near OE = 0, not a coverage diagnostic: flagged and unflagged draws cover alike at every threshold tried; it no longer warns. The printed label tracks which construction produced the interval.

ward_residual(data.frame(A, M, Y = Yi, C), se_method = "bootstrap", B = 200)
#> Gauge-calibrated proportion mediated (onestep-crossfit, n=1500)
#>   P_med = 0.322  percentile [0.266, 0.384]
#>     Fieller 95% CI [0.264, 0.381]
#>   W=R/OE = 0.444  percentile [0.337, 0.535]  (p=2.36e-17)
#>   OE=1.423  IDE=0.333  IIE=0.459  R=0.632
#>   ! |W| large: additive split unreliable; interpret P_med with care.

For the near-null / weak-identification regime — OE not bounded away from 0 — the ratio itself is non-regular: in the grid’s near-null cells even an oracle with known nuisances produces exploding standard errors, and oe_regular = FALSE flags exactly this. Prefer the Fieller confidence set there (fieller = TRUE, on by default), which is honest about being unbounded when the total effect is not significant, and report the unnormalized effects.

Summary

  • ward_residual() reports P_med together with the gauge residual W = R/OE; W flags when the additive direct/indirect split — and therefore the single-number P_med — is unreliable.
  • Use a0 / a1 for any two-level exposure coding; >2 levels is an error by design.
  • For ratio inference, the default analytic Wald interval is calibrated under regular identification (0.936 continuous / 0.972 binary at n = 800); reps > 1 adds a small efficiency gain; se_method = "bootstrap" gives percentile intervals that are no better (0.905–0.930) and its weak_id flag is not a coverage diagnostic; oe_regular and the Fieller set handle the near-null case, where the ratio is non-regular.
